readings.c2s1:
¶
'''uncommon''' (un-kom′ọn), ''adv.'' [< ''uncommon'', ''a.''] Exceedingly; very: as, ''uncommon'' cheap. [Vulgar.]

'''uncommonly''' (un-kom′ọn-li), ''adv.'' '''1.''' In an uncommon manner; rarely; not usually.
{{smaller block|We are not ''uncommonly'' told that Henry VII. had not in his own person the shadow of hereditary right.
{{right|''Stubbs'', Medieval and Modern Hist., p. 343.}}}}
'''2.''' To an uncommon degree.
{{smaller block|A boy who ’s ''uncommonly'' sharp of his age.
{{right|''Barham'', Ingoldsby Legends, I. 54.}}}}

'''uncommonness''' (un-kom′ọn-nes), ''n.'' The state or character of being uncommon; rareness of occurrence; infrequency.

'''uncommunicable''' (un-kọ-mū′ni-ka-bl), ''a.'' '''1.''' Incommunicable. ''Burke.''—'''2.''' Not communicative; reserved; taciturn. ''Imp. Dict.'' [Rare.]

'''uncommunicated''' (un-kọ-mū′ni-kā-ted), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not communicated; not disclosed or made known to others.—'''2.''' Not imparted or bestowed: as, the ''uncommunicated'' perfections of God. ''Waterland.''—'''3.''' Not having received the communion.

'''uncommunicative''' (un-kọ-mū′ni-kā-tiv), ''a.'' '''1†.''' Not communicative or disposed to impart one’s wealth; not liberal; parsimonious.
{{smaller block|A little too ''uncommunicative'' for their great circumstances.
{{right|''Richardson'', Clarissa Harlowe, ii. 90.}}}}
'''2.''' Not communicative; not disposed to impart one’s thoughts; not free to communicate to others; reserved; taciturn.
{{smaller block|A churlish and ''uncommunicative'' disposition.
{{right|''Chesterfield.''}}}}

'''uncommunicativeness''' (un-kọ-mū′ni-kā-tiv-
readings.c2s2:
nes), ''n.'' The state or character of being uncommunicative, reserved, or taciturn; reserve. ''Richardson.''

'''uncompact''' (un-kọm-pakt′), ''a.'' Incompact. ''Addison.''

'''uncompacted''' (un-kọm-pak′ted), ''a.'' Not compact; not firm or settled. ''Feltham.''

'''uncompanied''' (un-kum′pa̤-nid), ''a.'' Having no companion; unaccompanied. ''Fairfax.''

'''uncompanionable''' (un-kọm-pan′yọn-a-bl), ''a.'' Not companionable or sociable. ''Miss Burney.''

'''uncompanioned''' (un-kọm-pan′yọnd), ''a.'' Unaccompanied; without a companion; alone; solitary; having no equal.
{{smaller block|In his hours of ''uncompanioned'' darkness.
{{right|''J. Wilson'', Lights and Shadows of Scottish Life.}}}}

'''uncompassionate''' (un-kọm-pash′ọn-ạ̄t), ''a.'' Not compassionate; having no pity. ''Milton'', S. A., l. 818.

'''uncompatibly†''' (un-kọm-pat′i-bli), ''adv.'' Incompatibly. ''Imp. Dict.''

'''uncompellable''' (un-kọm-pel′a̤-bl), ''a.'' That cannot be forced or compelled. ''Feltham.''

'''uncomplaining''' (un-kọm-plā′ning), ''a.'' Not complaining; not murmuring; not disposed to murmur; submissive.
{{smaller block|<poem>Let thy loud heart keep,
Like his, a mute and ''uncomplaining'' sleep.</poem>
{{right|''Shelley'', Adonais, iii.}}}}
readings.c2s3:
¶
'''uncomplainingly''' (un-kọm-plā′ning-li), ''adv.'' In an uncomplaining manner; without murmuring or complaint.

'''uncomplaisant''' (un-kom′plạ̄-zant), ''a.'' Not complaisant; not civil; not courteous. ''Locke.''

'''uncomplaisantly''' (un-kom′plạ̄-zant-li), ''adv.'' Uncivilly; discourteously. ''Blackstone.''

'''uncompliable''' (un-kọm-plī′ạ-bl), ''a.'' Unready or unwilling to yield or comply. ''Cudworth,'' Morality, IV. v. § 3.

'''uncompliant''' (un-kọm-plī′ạnt), ''a.'' Incompliant. ''Bp. Gauden.''

'''uncomposable''' (un-kọm-pō′zạ-bl), ''a.'' Incapable of being composed; not to be reconciled or arranged. ''Roger North,'' Examen, p. 63.

'''uncompounded''' (un-kọm-poun′ded), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not compounded; not mixed; simple.
{{smaller block|<poem>For spirits, when they please,
Can either sex assume, or both; so soft
And ''uncompounded'' is their essence pure.</poem>
{{right|''Milton,'' P. L., i. 425.}}}}
'''2.''' Not intricate or complicated.
{{smaller block|That ''uncompounded'' style.
{{right|''Hammond,'' On Fundamentals.}}}}

'''uncomprehensible†''' (un-kom-prẹ̄-hen′si-bl), ''a.'' Incomprehensible. ''Bp. Jewell.''

'''uncomprehensive''' (un-kom-prẹ̄-hen′siv), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not comprehensive; not including much.—'''2†.''' Unable to comprehend; incomprehensive.
{{smaller block|Narrow-spirited, ''uncomprehensive'' zealots. {{right|''South.''}}}}
'''3†.''' Incomprehensible.
{{smaller block|<poem>The providence that ’s in a watchful state
Knows almost every grain of Plutus’ gold,
Finds bottom in the ''uncomprehensive'' deeps.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.,'' T. and C., iii. 3. 198.}}}}
readings.c3s1:
¶
'''uncompromising''' (un-kom′prọ̄-mī-zing), ''a.'' Not compromising; admitting of no compromise; not complying; inflexible; unyielding: as, ''uncompromising'' hostility. ''Macaulay'', Hallam’s Const. Hist.

'''unconable†''', ''a.'' See ''uncovenable.''

'''unconand†''', ''a.'' See ''uncunning.''

'''unconceiled†''', ''a.'' An obsolete variant of ''uncounseled.''

'''unconceivable†''' (un-kọn-sē′vạ-bl), ''a.'' Inconceivable. ''Locke.''

'''unconceivableness†''' (un-kọn-sē′vạ-bl-nes), ''n.'' Inconceivableness. ''Dr. H. More'', Immortal. of Soul, i. 4.

'''unconceivably†''' (un-kọn-sē′vạ-bli), ''adv.'' Inconceivably. ''Locke.''

'''unconcern''' (un-kọn-sėrn′), ''n.'' Want of concern; absence of anxiety; freedom from solicitude; indifferentism; indifference; apathy.
{{smaller block|I can’t bear to hear her spoken of with Levity or ''Unconcern.'' {{right|''Steele'', Conscious Lovers, ii. 1.}}}}
='''Syn.''' ''Indifference, Insensibility'', etc. {{smaller|See ''apathy.''}}

'''unconcerned''' (un-kọn-sėrnd′), ''a.'' Not concerned; not anxious; feeling no concern or solicitude; easy in mind; not interested; not affected.
{{smaller block|<poem>The morn,
All ''unconcern’d'' with our unrest.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., xi. 174.}}
Calm Villain! how ''unconcern’d'' he stands, confessing Treachery and Ingratitude!
{{right|''Congreve'', Double-Dealer, i. 6.}}}}
='''Syn.''' ''Unconcerned at, for, about.'' {{smaller|With ''at'', ''unconcerned'' means not anxious in view of something that is or happens; with ''for'' it means not anxious for the safety or}}
readings.c3s2:
{{smaller|success of some object of interest or desire: ''unconcerned at'' the successes of a rival; ''unconcerned for'' one’s own safety. With ''about'' it generally means the same as with ''for'', but sometimes the same as with ''at''.}}

'''unconcernedly''' (un-kọn-sėr′ned-li), ''adv.'' In an unconcerned manner; without concern or anxiety.

'''unconcernedness''' (un-kọn-sėr′ned-nes), ''n.'' Freedom from concern or anxiety. ''South.''

'''unconcerning†''' (un-kọn-sėr′ning), ''a.'' Not interesting; not affecting; not belonging to one. ''Dr. H. More.''

'''unconcernment''' (un-kọn-sėrn′mẹnt), ''n.'' The state of having no interest or concern. ''South.''

'''unconcludent†''' (un-kọn-klö′dent), ''a.'' Not decisive; inconclusive. ''Sir M. Hale.''

'''unconcludible†''' (un-kọn-klö′di-bl), ''a.'' Not to be concluded or determined.
{{smaller block|That which is ''unconcludible'' . . . to the understanding.
{{right|''Dr. H. More'', Philos. Poems, notes.}}}}

'''unconcluding†''' (un-kọn-klö′ding), ''a.'' Inconclusive.
{{smaller block|False and ''unconcluding'' reasonings.
{{right|''Locke.''}}}}

'''unconcludingness†''' (un-kọn-klö′ding-nes), ''n.'' The character of being inconclusive.
{{smaller block|The uncertainty of the truth, . . . by reason of the ''unconcludingness'' of the arguments brought to attest it.
{{right|''Jer. Taylor'', Works (ed. 1835), II. 344.}}}}

'''unconclusive†''' (un-kọn-klö′siv), ''a.'' Inconclusive. ''Hammond.''
readings.c3s3:
¶
'''unconcocted''' (un-kọn-kok′ted), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not concocted; not digested. ''Sir T. Browne.''—'''2.''' Figuratively, crude; indigested.

'''unconcurrent''' (un-kọn-kur′e̤nt), ''a.'' Not concurring or agreeing. ''Daniel.''

'''uncondemned''' (un-kọn-demd′), ''a.'' Not condemned; not judged guilty; not disapproved; not pronounced criminal.
{{smaller block|They have beaten us openly ''uncondemned.'' {{right|Acts xvi. 37.}}
A familiar and ''uncondemned'' practice. {{right|''Locke.''}}}}

'''uncondited†''' (un-kọn-dī′ted), ''a.'' [< ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + L. ''conditus'', pp. of ''condire'', season, spice, flavor.] Unseasoned. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|While he estimates the secrets of religion by such measures, they must needs seem as insipid as cork, or the ''uncondited'' mushroom. {{right|''Jer. Taylor'', Works (ed. 1835), II. 60.}}}}

'''unconditional''' (un-kọn-dish′ọn-ạl), ''a.'' Not conditional; absolute; unreserved; not limited by any conditions: as, an ''unconditional'' surrender.
{{smaller block|<poem>O pass not, Lord, an absolute decree,
Or bind thy sentence ''unconditional.''</poem>
{{right|''Dryden'', Annus Mirabilis.}}}}

'''unconditionality''' (un-kọn-dish-ọn-al′i-ti), ''n.'' The character or state of being unconditional. ''J. Ward'', Encyc. Brit., XX. 82.

'''unconditionally''' (un-kọn-dish′ọn-ạl-i), ''adv.'' In an unconditional manner; without conditions: as, to surrender ''unconditionally.''

'''unconditionalness''' (un-kọn-dish′ọn-ạl-nes), ''n.'' The character of being unconditional. ''J. Fiske'', Cosmic Philos., I. 151.

'''unconditioned''' (un-kọn-dish′ọnd), ''a.'' Not subject to conditions; not an effect, accident, or result of circumstances.

'''uncomeatable''' (un-kum-at′a-bl), ''a.'' [< ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''come-at-able.''] Not accessible; not attainable; beyond reach or comprehension. [Colloq.]
{{smaller block|He has a perfect art in being unintelligible in discourse, and ''uncomeatable'' in business. {{right|''Steele'', Tatler, No. 12.}}}}

'''uncomeliness''' (un-kum′li-nes), ''n.'' '''1.''' Want of comeliness; want of beauty or grace: as, ''uncomeliness'' of person, of dress, or behavior.—'''2.''' Unbecomingness; unseemliness; indecency.
{{smaller block|He . . . gave such orderly and well-behaved reproof to all ''uncomeliness'' that I would have sworn his disposition would have gone to the truth of his words. {{right|''Shak.'', M. W. of W., ii. 1. 60.}}}}

'''uncomely''' (un-kum′li), ''a.'' [< ME. ''uncomely'', ''oncomely'', ''uncumelich'' ; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''comely.''] '''1.''' Not comely; wanting grace: as, an ''uncomely'' person; ''uncomely'' dress.—'''2.''' Unseemly; unbecoming; unsuitable; indecent.
{{smaller block|Thinke nothing ''uncomly'' which is honest, for nothing is comely that is not honest. {{right|''Booke of Precedence'' (E. E. T. S., extra ser.), i. 71.}}}}
{{smaller block|Besides (to say truth) nakedness is ''uncomely'', as well in mind as in body. {{right|''Bacon.''}}}}

'''uncomely†''' (un-kum′li), ''adv.'' In an uncomely or unbecoming manner; indecently. 1 Cor. vii. 36.
{{smaller block|’Tis most ''uncomely'' spoken. {{right|''Fletcher'' (''and Massinger'' ?), False One, iii. 1.}}}}

'''uncomfortable''' (un-kum′fėr-tạ-bl), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not comfortable; affording no comfort; causing bodily or mental discomfort; giving uneasiness; disquieting: as, an ''uncomfortable'' seat or condition.

{{smaller block|Christmas is in the most dead and the most ''uncomfortable'' time of the year. {{right|''Addison.''}}
How ''uncomfortable'' will the remembrance be of all your excesses, oaths, injustice and profaneness, when death approaches, and judgment follows it? {{right|''Stillingfleet'', Sermons, I. v.}}}}
'''2.''' Disagreeably situated; uneasy; ill at ease: as, to feel ''uncomfortable.''
{{smaller block|<poem>How surely dost thou malice these extremes,
''Uncomfortable'' man. {{right|''Ford'', Lady’s Trial, iii. 3.}}</poem>}}

'''uncomfortableness''' (un-kum′fėr-ta̤-bl-nes), ''n.'' The state of being uncomfortable, uneasy, or miserable. ''Jer. Taylor.''

'''uncomfortably''' (un-kum′fėr-ta̤-bli), ''adv.'' In an uncomfortable manner; with discomfort or uneasiness; in an uneasy state.

'''uncommendable''' (un-kọ-men′da̤-bl), ''a.'' Not commendable; not worthy of commendation; illaudable. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|The ''uncommendable'' licentiousness of his poetry. {{right|''Feltham'', On Eccles. ii. 11.}}}}

'''uncommerciable''' (un-kọ-mėr′shia̤-bl), ''a.'' [< ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + *''commerciable'', equiv. to ''commerceable.''] Not capable of being made an article of commerce. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|By prohibiting all his Majesty’s subjects from dealing in tobacco, one third of the exports of the United States are rendered ''uncommerciable'' here. {{right|''Thos. Jefferson'', To Count De Montmorin (Works, II. 188).}}}}

'''uncommercial''' (un-kọ-mėr′sha̤l), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not commercial; not carrying on or familiar with or devoted to commerce.
{{smaller block|The ''Uncommercial'' Traveller. {{right|''Dickens.''}} The wisdom of taking measures to keep the river in good condition is made plain to even the ''uncommercial'' mind. {{right|''S. L. Clemens'', Life on the Mississippi, p. 310.}}}}

'''2.''' Not in accordance with the principles of commerce.

{{smaller block|You did not think it ''uncommercial'' to tax the whole mass of your manufactures, and, let me add, your agriculture too. {{right|''Burke'', American Taxation. (''Encyc. Dict.'')}}}}

'''uncommitted''' (un-kọ-mit′ed), ''a.'' [< ME. ''uncommitted''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''committed''.] '''1.''' Not committed or done.

{{smaller block|Offys ''uncommitted'' ofte anoyeth. {{right|''Chaucer'', Parliament of Fowls, l. 518.}}
The ''uncommitted'' sin. {{right|''Hammond.''}}}}

'''2.''' Not committed or intrusted.—'''3.''' Not referred to a committee.—'''4.''' Not pledged by anything said or done: as, ''uncommitted'' by rash promises or statements; an ''uncommitted'' delegation to a convention.

'''uncommixed†''' (un-kọ-mikst′), ''a.'' Not commixed or mingled. ''Chapman.''

'''uncommon''' (un-kom′ọn), ''a.'' Not common; not usual; infrequent; rare; hence, remarkable; extraordinary; strange.

{{smaller block|I do not think it foreign to my design to speak of a man born in Her Majesty’s dominions, and relate an adventure in his life, so ''uncommon'' that it is doubtful whether the like has happened to any of human race. {{right|''Steele'', Englishman, No. 26.}}
The spiritual is ever foreign to the material, the ''uncommon'' to the common. {{right|''W. Sharp'', D. G. Rossetti, iii.}}}}

{{smaller|='''Syn.''' Scarce, unusual, unwonted, unique, singular, queer. See ''common''.}}

'''uncommon''' (un-kom′ọn), ''adv.'' [< ''uncommon'', ''a.''] Exceedingly; very: as, ''uncommon'' cheap. [Vulgar.]

'''uncommonly''' (un-kom′ọn-li), ''adv.'' '''1.''' In an uncommon manner; rarely; not usually.
{{smaller block|We are not ''uncommonly'' told that Henry VII. had not in his own person the shadow of hereditary right.
{{right|''Stubbs'', Medieval and Modern Hist., p. 343.}}}}
'''2.''' To an uncommon degree.
{{smaller block|A boy who ’s ''uncommonly'' sharp of his age.
{{right|''Barham'', Ingoldsby Legends, I. 54.}}}}

{{smaller block|In his hours of ''uncompanioned'' darkness.
{{right|''J. Wilson'', Lights and Shadows of Scottish Life.}}}}

'''uncompassionate''' (un-kọm-pash′ọn-ạ̄t), ''a.'' Not compassionate; having no pity. ''Milton'', S. A., l. 818.

'''uncompatibly†''' (un-kọm-pat′i-bli), ''adv.'' Incompatibly. ''Imp. Dict.''

'''uncompellable''' (un-kọm-pel′a̤-bl), ''a.'' That cannot be forced or compelled. ''Feltham.''

'''uncompliant''' (un-kọm-plī′ạnt), ''a.'' Incompliant. ''Bp. Gauden.''

With ''about'' it generally means the same as with ''for'', but sometimes the same as with ''at''.}}

{{smaller block|They have beaten us openly ''uncondemned.'' {{right|Acts xvi. 37.}}

'''uncondited†''' (un-kọn-dī′ted), ''a.'' [< ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + L. ''conditus'', pp. of ''condire'', season, spice, flavor.] Unseasoned. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|While he estimates the secrets of religion by such measures, they must needs seem as insipid as cork, or the ''uncondited'' mushroom. {{right|''Jer. Taylor'', Works (ed. 1835), II. 60.}}}}

'''unconditional''' (un-kọn-dish′ọn-ạl), ''a.'' Not conditional; absolute; unreserved; not limited by any conditions: as, an ''unconditional'' surrender.
{{smaller block|<poem>O pass not, Lord, an absolute decree,
Or bind thy sentence ''unconditional.''</poem>
{{right|''Dryden'', Annus Mirabilis.}}}}

'''unconditionality''' (un-kọn-dish-ọn-al′i-ti), ''n.'' The character or state of being unconditional. ''J. Ward'', Encyc. Brit., XX. 82.

'''unconditionally''' (un-kọn-dish′ọn-ạl-i), ''adv.'' In an unconditional manner; without conditions: as, to surrender ''unconditionally.''

'''unconditionalness''' (un-kọn-dish′ọn-ạl-nes), ''n.'' The character of being unconditional. ''J. Fiske'', Cosmic Philos., I. 151.

'''unconditioned''' (un-kọn-dish′ọnd), ''a.'' Not subject to conditions; not an effect, accident, or result of circumstances.<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
